topic: Introduction to OSHA: rights, duties and enforcement

notes.front: What is the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 (OSH Act)?
notes.back: The federal workplace safety and health law enacted by Public Law 91–596 on 29 December 1970; it is chapter 15 of Title 29, U.S. Code.
notes.explanation: Section 1 of that public law gave the Act its short title and enacted the chapter.
notes.example: Like a parent law for a whole shelf of rules: the construction rules in Part 1926 are one of the rule books made under it.
introduces: Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 651 note (short title), p. 2
notes.evidence: Pub. L. 91–596, § 1, Dec. 29, 1970, 84 Stat. 1590, provided: ‘‘That this Act [enacting this chapter
uses: Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970

notes.front: What is the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)?
notes.back: The agency of the U.S. Department of Labor whose authorised officers inspect workplaces under the OSH Act.
notes.explanation: Part 1903 defines its inspectors, Compliance Safety and Health Officers, as persons OSHA authorises to conduct inspections.
notes.example: Like a traffic police force for workplace safety laws, but it also writes the notice every employer must put up.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.22(d), p. 17
notes.evidence: Compliance Safety and Health Officer means a person authorized by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, U.S. Department of Labor, to conduct inspections.

notes.front: What is the general duty clause of the OSH Act?
notes.back: Section 5(a)(1): each employer must provide employment and a workplace free from recognised hazards causing or likely to cause death or serious physical harm.
notes.explanation: It applies to every employer and stands beside the separate duty in section 5(a)(2) to comply with specific standards.
notes.example: Like a catch-all rule in a club’s constitution, but it reaches only recognised hazards that could kill or seriously harm.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 654(a)(1), p. 4
notes.evidence: shall furnish to each of his employees employment and a place of employment which are free from recognized hazards that are causing or are likely to cause death or serious physical harm to his employees

notes.front: What is anti-retaliation protection under section 11(c) of the OSH Act?
notes.back: A ban on any person discharging or discriminating against an employee for filing a complaint, testifying or exercising any right under the Act.
notes.explanation: The protection reaches anyone who complains, starts a proceeding, testifies or uses any other right the Act gives.
notes.example: Like a whistle-blower shield, but for safety complaints and other rights under the OSH Act.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 660(c)(1), p. 13
notes.evidence: No person shall discharge or in any manner discriminate against any employee because such employee has filed any complaint or instituted or caused to be instituted any proceeding under or related to this chapter

notes.front: What is a Compliance Safety and Health Officer (CSHO)?
notes.back: A person authorised by OSHA, U.S. Department of Labor, to conduct inspections.
notes.explanation: Part 1903 puts the officer in charge of inspections and of questioning people during them.
notes.example: Like a building inspector who arrives at the site, but checking compliance with safety and health rules.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.22(d), p. 17
notes.evidence: Compliance Safety and Health Officer means a person authorized by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, U.S. Department of Labor, to conduct inspections.

notes.front: What is a citation under the OSH Act?
notes.back: A written notice to an employer describing with particularity an alleged violation, the provision violated and a reasonable time for abatement.
notes.explanation: The Act requires one to be issued with reasonable promptness when an inspection shows the employer has violated a duty, standard, rule or regulation.
notes.example: Like a parking ticket that names the rule broken, but it also sets a deadline to fix the hazard.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 658(a), p. 11
notes.evidence: he shall with reasonable promptness issue a citation to the employer. Each citation shall be in writing

notes.front: What is a de minimis violation?
notes.back: A violation with no direct or immediate relationship to safety or health, for which a notice may be issued instead of a citation.
notes.explanation: The Act lets the Secretary prescribe procedures for such a notice in lieu of a citation.
notes.example: Like a technical slip on paperwork that changes nothing about how safe the work is.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 658(a), p. 12
notes.evidence: the issuance of a notice in lieu of a citation with respect to de minimis violations which have no direct or immediate relationship to safety or health

notes.front: What is a serious violation under the OSH Act?
notes.back: One where there is a substantial probability that death or serious physical harm could result from a condition or practice in the workplace.
notes.explanation: The Act adds an exception: not if the employer did not, and could not with reasonable diligence, know of the violation.
notes.example: Like an unguarded floor edge on the fifth storey, where a fall could well kill.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 666(k), p. 16
notes.evidence: a serious violation shall be deemed to exist in a place of employment if there is a substantial probability that death or serious physical harm could result from a condition which exists

notes.front: What is a willful violation, in the OSH Act’s penalty scheme?
notes.back: A violation the employer commits willfully; it is the only category with a minimum penalty as well as a maximum.
notes.explanation: Section 17(a) of the Act covers employers who willfully or repeatedly violate, and sets a floor only for each willful violation.
notes.example: Like a driver who knows the speed limit and ignores it on purpose, rather than by mistake.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 666(a), p. 16
notes.evidence: may be assessed a civil penalty of not more than $70,000 for each violation, but not less than $5,000 for each willful violation

notes.front: What is a repeated violation, in the OSH Act’s penalty scheme?
notes.back: A violation by an employer who repeatedly violates the Act’s requirements; it has the willful violation’s maximum penalty but no minimum.
notes.explanation: Section 17(a) groups employers who willfully or repeatedly violate; the minimum applies only to each willful violation.
notes.example: Like being fined again for the same kind of breach you were fined for before.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 666(a), p. 16
notes.evidence: Any employer who willfully or repeatedly violates the requirements of section 654 of this title, any standard, rule, or order promulgated pursuant to section 655 of this title, or regulations prescribed pursuant to this chapter may be assessed a civil penalty of not more than $70,000 for each violation, but not less than $5,000 for each willful violation.

notes.front: What is an other-than-serious violation?
notes.back: A cited violation specifically determined not to be of a serious nature.
notes.explanation: Section 17(c) of the Act lets a penalty be assessed for it, but does not require one.
notes.example: Like a missing label on a first-aid cabinet: a real breach, but unlikely to kill or seriously harm anyone.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 666(c), p. 16
notes.evidence: such violation is specifically determined not to be of a serious nature, may be assessed a civil penalty of up to $7,000 for each such violation

notes.front: What is the Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission (OSHRC)?
notes.back: A commission created by the OSH Act to carry out its adjudicatory functions, such as deciding contested citations.
notes.explanation: The Act creates it in the same clause that gives the Secretary of Labor the power to set standards, so judging and rule-making sit apart.
notes.example: Like a tribunal that hears appeals against fines, separate from the agency that issued them.
introduces: Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 651(b)(3), p. 1
notes.evidence: by authorizing the Secretary of Labor to set mandatory occupational safety and health standards applicable to businesses affecting interstate commerce, and by creating an Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission for carrying out adjudicatory functions under this chapter
uses: Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission

notes.front: What is an imminent danger under the OSH Act?
notes.back: A danger that could reasonably be expected to cause death or serious physical harm immediately, or before normal enforcement could remove it.
notes.explanation: For such dangers the Act lets the Secretary ask a federal district court to restrain the conditions or practices.
notes.example: Like a live power line lying across a walkway that people are using right now.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 662(a), p. 15
notes.evidence: a danger exists which could reasonably be expected to cause death or serious physical harm immediately or before the imminence of such danger can be eliminated through the enforcement procedures otherwise provided by this chapter

notes.front: What is a state plan under the OSH Act?
notes.back: A state’s plan to take over developing and enforcing its own safety and health standards on issues covered by federal standards.
notes.explanation: A state must submit the plan to the Secretary of Labor; its standards must be at least as effective as the federal ones.
notes.example: Like a franchise run locally under the head office’s minimum rules.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 667(b), p. 17
notes.evidence: Any State which, at any time, desires to assume responsibility for development and enforcement therein of occupational safety and health standards

notes.front: The OSH Act’s stated purpose is to assure so far as possible every working man and woman in the Nation {{c1::safe and healthful working conditions}}.
notes.explanation: Congress grounds the purpose in its powers to regulate commerce and to provide for the general welfare.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 651(b), p. 1
notes.evidence: through the exercise of its powers to regulate commerce among the several States and with foreign nations and to provide for the general welfare, to assure so far as possible every working man and woman in the Nation safe and healthful working conditions

notes.front: Under the OSH Act, who is authorised to set mandatory occupational safety and health standards?
notes.back: The Secretary of Labor.
notes.explanation: The same clause hands adjudication to a separate Review Commission, so setting standards and judging disputes sit with different bodies.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 651(b)(3), p. 1
notes.evidence: by authorizing the Secretary of Labor to set mandatory occupational safety and health standards applicable to businesses affecting interstate commerce, and by creating an Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission for carrying out adjudicatory functions
uses: Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission

notes.front: Besides the general duty clause, what second duty does section 5(a) of the OSH Act place on each employer?
notes.back: To comply with occupational safety and health standards promulgated under the Act.
notes.explanation: Section 5(a)(2) makes the specific standards, such as the construction rules in Part 1926, binding on the employer in their own right.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 654(a)(2), p. 4
notes.evidence: (2) shall comply with occupational safety and health standards promulgated under this chapter.

notes.front: What duty does section 5(b) of the OSH Act place on each employee?
notes.back: To comply with the standards, rules, regulations and orders under the Act that apply to his or her own actions and conduct.
notes.explanation: The duty is limited to rules that apply to the employee’s own conduct; the workplace-wide duties in section 5(a) fall on the employer.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 654(b), p. 4
notes.evidence: Each employee shall comply with occupational safety and health standards and all rules, regulations, and orders issued pursuant to this chapter which are applicable to his own actions and conduct.

notes.front: Under section 8(f) of the OSH Act, when may employees or their representative request an inspection?
notes.back: When they believe a violation of a standard that threatens physical harm exists, or that an imminent danger exists.
notes.explanation: They do so by giving notice of the violation or danger to the Secretary or his authorised representative.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 657(f)(1), p. 11
notes.evidence: Any employees or representative of employees who believe that a violation of a safety or health standard exists that threatens physical harm, or that an imminent danger exists, may request an inspection

notes.front: What three things must an employee’s notice requesting an inspection be?
notes.back: Reduced to writing; setting out the grounds with reasonable particularity; signed by the employees or their representative.
notes.explanation: Part 1903 lets the notice go to the Area Director or to a Compliance Safety and Health Officer.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.11(a), p. 6
notes.evidence: Any such notice shall be reduced to writing, shall set forth with reasonable particularity the grounds for the notice, and shall be signed by the employee or representative of employees.

notes.front: Can an employee who requests an inspection keep their name off the copy of the notice given to the employer?
notes.back: Yes: on the request of the person giving notice, their name and those of employees referred to must not appear on it.
notes.explanation: The employer does get a copy of the notice, no later than the time of inspection, but without those names if asked.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 657(f)(1), p. 11
notes.evidence: upon the request of the person giving such notice, his name and the names of individual employees referred to therein shall not appear in such copy

notes.front: Within how many days of the violation must an employee file a section 11(c) retaliation complaint with the Secretary of Labor?
notes.back: Thirty days.
notes.explanation: The Secretary then investigates and, if the subsection was violated, brings an action in a United States district court.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 660(c)(2), p. 13
notes.evidence: may, within thirty days after such violation occurs, file a complaint with the Secretary alleging such discrimination

notes.front: What relief can a district court order for an employee who suffered retaliation under section 11(c)?
notes.back: All appropriate relief, including rehiring or reinstatement to the former position with back pay.
notes.explanation: The court acts on an action brought by the Secretary after investigating the complaint.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 660(c)(2), p. 13
notes.evidence: order all appropriate relief including rehiring or reinstatement of the employee to his former position with back pay

notes.front: Does section 11(c) forbid retaliation only by the worker’s own employer?
notes.back: No. It says “no person”, and the Act defines a person widely, so its prohibitions are not limited to employers.
notes.explanation: Part 1977 points to the Act’s definition of person: individuals, partnerships, associations, corporations and other groups.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1977 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1977.4, p. 3
notes.evidence: Consequently, the prohibitions of section 11(c) are not limited to actions taken by employer

notes.front: According to Part 1977, when is an employee who refuses to expose himself to a dangerous condition protected from discrimination?
notes.back: When, with no reasonable alternative, he refuses in good faith, facing a real danger of death or serious injury.
notes.explanation: Part 1977 also requires that there be insufficient time, because of urgency, to remove the danger through regular enforcement channels.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1977 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1977.12(b)(2), p. 5
notes.evidence: If the employee, with no reasonable alternative, refuses in good faith to expose himself to the dangerous condition, he would be protected against subsequent discrimination.

notes.front: Where must an employer post the notice furnished by OSHA that informs employees of their protections and obligations?
notes.back: In each establishment, in a conspicuous place where notices to employees are customarily posted.
notes.explanation: The employer must also keep it from being altered, defaced or covered by other material.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.2(a)(1), p. 2
notes.evidence: Such notice or notices shall be posted by the employer in each establishment in a conspicuous place or places where notices to employees are customarily posted.

notes.front: On presenting credentials, when may the Secretary’s representative enter a construction site to inspect it?
notes.back: Without delay and at reasonable times.
notes.explanation: The Act names construction sites among the workplaces covered, and allows inspection during regular working hours and other reasonable times.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 657(a)(1), p. 10
notes.evidence: to enter without delay and at reasonable times any factory, plant, establishment, construction site, or other area, workplace or environment where work is performed by an employee of an employer

notes.front: May OSHA give an employer advance notice of an inspection?
notes.back: Not as a rule; only in listed situations, such as apparent imminent danger, so the employer can abate it quickly.
notes.explanation: Other listed cases include inspections after hours and ensuring representatives are present; the Area Director must usually authorise it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.6(a), p. 4
notes.evidence: Advance notice of inspections may not be given, except in the following situations: (1) In cases of apparent imminent danger, to enable the employer to abate the danger as quickly as possible

notes.front: Under section 1926.3 of the construction rules, what is a condition of each contract subject to section 107 of the Contract Work Hours and Safety Standards Act?
notes.back: That the Secretary of Labor or an authorised representative has a right of entry to any site of contract performance.
notes.explanation: The entry is for inspecting compliance with the construction standards and carrying out the Secretary’s duties under section 107.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.3(a), p. 6
notes.evidence: It shall be a condition of each contract which is subject to section 107 of the Contract Work Hours and Safety Standards Act that the Secretary of Labor or any authorized representative shall have a right of entry to any site of contract performance

notes.front: What must a CSHO do at the beginning of an inspection?
notes.back: Present credentials to the person in charge; explain the nature and purpose of the inspection; indicate its general scope and the records to review.
notes.explanation: Part 1903 adds that naming records at the start does not stop the officer asking for others later.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.7(a), p. 4
notes.evidence: Compliance Safety and Health Officers shall present their credentials to the owner, operator, or agent in charge at the establishment; explain the nature and purpose of the inspection

notes.front: What happens at the end of an inspection, under section 1903.7(e)?
notes.back: The CSHO confers with the employer and informally advises of any apparent violations found.
notes.explanation: The employer may use that conference to bring pertinent information about workplace conditions to the officer’s attention.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.7(e), p. 5
notes.evidence: At the conclusion of an inspection, the Compliance Safety and Health Officer shall confer with the employer or his representative and informally advise him of any apparent safety or health violations disclosed by the inspection.

notes.front: Who must be given an opportunity to accompany the CSHO during the physical inspection of a workplace?
notes.back: A representative of the employer and a representative authorised by the employees.
notes.explanation: Part 1903 says the purpose is to aid the inspection; the officer may allow more than one of each.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.8(a), p. 5
notes.evidence: A representative of the employer and a representative authorized by his employees shall be given an opportunity to accompany the Compliance Safety and Health Officer during the physical inspection of any workplace

notes.front: What must the CSHO do if there is no authorised employee representative?
notes.back: Consult a reasonable number of employees about safety and health in the workplace.
notes.explanation: The same applies if the officer cannot tell with reasonable certainty who the representative is.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.8(b), p. 5
notes.evidence: he shall consult with a reasonable number of employees concerning matters of safety and health in the workplace

notes.front: What does a CSHO do if the employer refuses entry or refuses to let the employee representative accompany the inspection?
notes.back: Terminates the inspection or confines it to areas and matters where no objection is raised.
notes.explanation: The same applies when the employer refuses to let the officer review records or question people.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.4(a), p. 3
notes.evidence: the Safety and Health Officer shall terminate the inspection or confine the inspection to other areas, conditions, structures

notes.front: Besides describing the violation, what must every citation fix?
notes.back: A reasonable time for abatement of the violation.
notes.explanation: The citation must also refer to the provision of the Act, standard, rule, regulation or order alleged to have been violated.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 658(a), p. 12
notes.evidence: In addition, the citation shall fix a reasonable time for the abatement of the violation.

notes.front: How long after a violation occurs can a citation still be issued?
notes.back: Up to six months; none may be issued after that.
notes.explanation: Part 1903 repeats the same six-month limit for citations issued by the Area Director.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 658(c), p. 12
notes.evidence: No citation may be issued under this section after the expiration of six months following the occurrence of any violation.

notes.front: Where must an employer post a citation on receiving it?
notes.back: Immediately, unedited, at or near each place where an alleged violation occurred.
notes.explanation: If that is not practicable, it goes in a prominent place where all affected employees will readily see it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.16(a), p. 10
notes.evidence: the employer shall immediately post such citation, or a copy thereof, unedited, at or near each place an alleged violation referred to in the citation occurred

notes.front: How long must a posted citation stay up?
notes.back: Until the violation has been abated, or for 3 working days, whichever is later.
notes.explanation: Whichever date is later governs, so a quick fix does not shorten the posting.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.16(b), p. 10
notes.evidence: Each citation, or a copy thereof, shall remain posted until the violation has been abated, or for 3 working days, whichever is later.

notes.front: A condition is not a serious violation if the employer did not, and could not with the exercise of {{c1::reasonable diligence}}, know of the violation.
notes.explanation: The definition therefore turns on both the likely harm and what the employer knew or could have known.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 666(k), p. 16
notes.evidence: unless the employer did not, and could not with the exercise of reasonable diligence, know of the presence of the violation

notes.front: What are two of the four factors the Area Director must consider in setting a proposed penalty?
notes.back: Any two of: size of the business; gravity of the violation; good faith of the employer; history of previous violations.
notes.explanation: Part 1903 requires due consideration of all four, in line with section 17 of the Act.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.15(b), p. 10
notes.evidence: giving due consideration to the appropriateness of the penalty with respect to the size of the business of the employer being charged, the gravity of the violation, the good faith of the employer, and the history of previous violations

notes.front: For penalties proposed after 15 January 2025, what are the minimum and maximum civil penalties per willful violation?
notes.back: At least $11,823 and at most $165,514.
notes.explanation: The Act itself still prints $5,000 and $70,000; Part 1903 lists the adjusted amounts for penalties proposed after that date.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.15(d)(1), p. 10
notes.evidence: The penalty per willful violation under section 17(a) of the Act, 29 U.S.C. 666(a), shall not be less than $11,823 and shall not exceed $165,514.

notes.front: For penalties proposed after 15 January 2025, what is the maximum civil penalty for a serious violation?
notes.explanation: Part 1903 sets the same ceiling for an other-than-serious violation; serious differs in having a penalty that must be assessed.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.15(d)(3), p. 10
notes.evidence: The penalty for a serious violation under section 17(b) of the Act, 29 U.S.C. 666(b), shall not exceed $16,550.

notes.front: For penalties proposed after 15 January 2025, what is the maximum penalty for failing to correct a cited violation?
notes.back: $16,550 per day.
notes.explanation: The Act counts each day the failure continues; the period does not start until the Commission’s final order when the employer contests in good faith.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.15(d)(5), p. 10
notes.evidence: The penalty for a failure to correct a violation under section 17(d) of the Act, 29 U.S.C. 666(d), shall not exceed $16,550 per day.

notes.front: What is the difference in wording between the OSH Act’s penalty for a serious violation and for an other-than-serious one?
notes.back: For a serious violation a penalty “shall be assessed”; for an other-than-serious one it “may be assessed”.
notes.explanation: Both are capped at the same figure; the difference is whether a penalty is mandatory.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 666(b), p. 16
notes.evidence: shall be assessed a civil penalty of up to $7,000 for each such violation

notes.front: How long does an employer have to notify the Secretary that it wishes to contest a citation or proposed penalty?
notes.back: Fifteen working days from receipt of the notice of proposed penalty.
notes.explanation: If it does not, and no employee files a notice, the citation and penalty become a final order of the Commission not reviewable by any court or agency.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 659(a), p. 12
notes.evidence: the employer has fifteen working days within which to notify the Secretary that he wishes to contest the citation or proposed assessment of penalty
uses: Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission

notes.front: What part of a citation may employees or their representative contest before the Review Commission?
notes.back: The period of time fixed for abatement, if they allege it is unreasonable.
notes.explanation: They file written notice with the Area Director, postmarked within 15 working days, as Part 1903 sets out.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.17(b), p. 11
notes.evidence: file a written notice with the Area Director alleging that the period of time fixed in the citation for the abatement of the violation is unreasonable
uses: Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission

notes.front: What must an inspector do as soon as he concludes that an imminent danger exists?
notes.back: Inform the affected employees and employers of the danger and that he is recommending the Secretary seek relief.
notes.explanation: The relief sought is a district court order, which can bar people from the place where the danger exists.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 662(c), p. 15
notes.evidence: he shall inform the affected employees and employers of the danger and that he is recommending to the Secretary that relief be sought

notes.front: A state plan’s standards must be {{c1::at least as effective}} as the federal standards on the same issues.
notes.explanation: This is one of the conditions the Secretary checks before approving a state plan.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 667(c)(2), p. 17
notes.evidence: at least as effective in providing safe and healthful employment and places of employment as the standards promulgated under section 655 of this title

notes.front: A contractor’s crew faces a recognised hazard that could cause serious physical harm, but no specific OSHA standard addresses it. Which provision can still require the employer to act?
notes.back: D: the general duty clause.
notes.choices:
A) Section 11(c)
B) Section 5(b), the employee duty
C) The de minimis provision
D) The general duty clause
notes.choicesExplained: B binds employees, not the employer. C covers breaches with no direct relationship to safety. A protects workers from retaliation; it sets no hazard duty.
notes.explanation: Section 5(a)(1) covers recognised hazards likely to cause death or serious physical harm, independently of the specific standards.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 654(a)(1), p. 4
notes.evidence: free from recognized hazards that are causing or are likely to cause death or serious physical harm to his employees

notes.front: A labourer removes the guard from his own saw despite the site rules and the standard requiring it. Whose duty under section 5 has he breached?
notes.back: C: his own, under section 5(b).
notes.choices:
A) Only the employer’s, because employees have no duties under the Act
B) The Review Commission’s
C) His own, under section 5(b)
D) Nobody’s, because only standards bind employers
notes.choicesExplained: A and D are wrong: section 5(b) gives employees their own duty. B: the Commission judges contests; it has no workplace duty.
notes.explanation: Section 5(b) makes each employee comply with standards and rules applicable to his own actions and conduct.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 654(b), p. 4
notes.evidence: Each employee shall comply with occupational safety and health standards and all rules, regulations, and orders issued pursuant to this chapter which are applicable to his own actions and conduct.
uses: Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission

notes.front: A roofer believes the site’s missing edge protection threatens physical harm and wants OSHA to inspect. What must his notice be?
notes.back: D: in writing, with reasonable particularity, and signed.
notes.choices:
A) A phone message with no details
B) Approved by the employer first
C) Anonymous and unwritten, or it will not be acted on
D) In writing, with reasonable particularity, and signed
notes.choicesExplained: A and C fail the writing and particularity rules. B: nothing requires employer approval; the employer only receives a copy.
notes.explanation: He can still ask for his name to be left off the employer’s copy, even though he signs the notice.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 657(f)(1), p. 11
notes.evidence: Any such notice shall be reduced to writing, shall set forth with reasonable particularity the grounds for the notice, and shall be signed by the employees or representative of employees

notes.front: A carpenter is sacked on 3 March, two days after testifying in an OSHA proceeding. By which date should she normally file her section 11(c) complaint?
notes.back: A: by 2 April, within thirty days.
notes.choices:
A) By 2 April, within thirty days
B) Within six months
C) Within 15 working days
D) Within 90 days
notes.choicesExplained: B is the limit for issuing citations. C is the time to contest a citation. D is the Secretary’s deadline to notify her of the determination.
notes.explanation: Section 11(c)(2) runs thirty days from when the violation occurs, here the dismissal on 3 March.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 660(c)(2), p. 13
notes.evidence: may, within thirty days after such violation occurs, file a complaint with the Secretary alleging such discrimination

notes.front: A worker is told to enter a trench whose wall is visibly collapsing. He asks the foreman to shore it, is refused, and declines to go in. Is his refusal protected?
notes.back: B: yes, if a reasonable person would see a real danger and there is no time to use regular enforcement.
notes.choices:
A) No, refusals are never protected
B) Yes, if a reasonable person would see a real danger and there is no time to use regular enforcement
C) Only if a CSHO is present on the site
D) Only if he first files a written complaint and waits
notes.choicesExplained: A contradicts Part 1977. D: the protection exists precisely where there is no time for enforcement channels. C: no officer needs to be present.
notes.explanation: He also sought correction from the employer and did not get it, which Part 1977 requires where possible.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1977 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1977.12(b)(2), p. 5
notes.evidence: there is a real danger of death or serious injury and that there is insufficient time, due to the urgency of the situation, to eliminate the danger through resort to regular statutory enforcement channels

notes.front: A site manager keeps the OSHA notice in a drawer in the site office and hands it to anyone who asks. Does this comply?
notes.back: A: no, it must be posted in a conspicuous place where notices are customarily posted.
notes.choices:
A) No, it must be posted in a conspicuous place where notices are customarily posted
B) Yes, as long as it is available on request
C) Yes, if it was shown at induction
D) No, it must be mailed to each employee
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the rule requires posting, not availability. D: nothing in Part 1903 requires mailing.
notes.explanation: Part 1903 requires the notice to be posted and kept posted.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.2(a)(1), p. 2
notes.evidence: Each employer shall post and keep posted a notice or notices, to be furnished by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration

notes.front: A CSHO arrives unannounced at a building site at 10 a.m. and shows credentials. The site agent asks her to come back next week. What does the Act authorise?
notes.back: C: she may enter without delay and at reasonable times.
notes.choices:
A) She must return by appointment
B) She may enter only if an employee complained
C) She may enter without delay and at reasonable times
D) She may enter only outside working hours
notes.choicesExplained: A reverses the rule; advance notice is itself restricted. B: the power of entry does not depend on a complaint. D: inspection during regular working hours is expressly allowed.
notes.explanation: Advance notice of inspections is itself restricted, so turning up unannounced is the normal case.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 657(a), p. 10
notes.evidence: upon presenting appropriate credentials to the owner, operator, or agent in charge, is authorized— (1) to enter without delay and at reasonable times

notes.front: During an inspection, the union’s authorised safety representative, who works for another firm, asks to join the walkaround. What should the CSHO do?
notes.back: A: allow it; the employees’ representative may be a third party.
notes.choices:
A) Allow it: the employees’ representative may be a third party
B) Refuse, as walkarounds are for the employer only
C) Postpone the inspection until he is employed on site
D) Refuse, as only the employer’s staff may attend
notes.choicesExplained: D and C: Part 1903 allows a third-party representative. B: the employees’ representative must be given the same opportunity as the employer’s.
notes.explanation: The opportunity to accompany is for the purpose of aiding the inspection.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.8(c), p. 5
notes.evidence: The representative(s) authorized by employees may be an employee of the employer or a third party.

notes.front: A citation for missing guardrails on level 4 is received on Monday; the guardrails are fixed on Tuesday. Where and until when must it be posted?
notes.back: B: near the level 4 violation, until at least the end of 3 working days.
notes.choices:
A) In the head office only, until the contest period ends
B) Near the level 4 violation, until at least the end of 3 working days
C) Nowhere, because the hazard was fixed
D) Near the violation, only until Tuesday
notes.choicesExplained: A: it goes at or near the place of violation. C: abatement does not remove the duty to post. D: it stays until abatement or 3 working days, whichever is later.
notes.explanation: The later of the two dates governs, so a fix on day two does not shorten the posting.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.16(b), p. 10
notes.evidence: shall remain posted until the violation has been abated, or for 3 working days, whichever is later

notes.front: An employer receives a notice of proposed penalty and does nothing for 20 working days; no employee files anything. What is the status of the citation?
notes.back: B: it is a final order of the Commission, not subject to review by any court or agency.
notes.choices:
A) Still open until the Review Commission rules
B) It is a final order of the Commission, not subject to review by any court or agency
C) Withdrawn automatically
D) Referred to a state plan
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Commission hears only contested cases. C: silence does not withdraw a citation. D: nothing in the contest procedure sends an uncontested citation to a state.
notes.explanation: The contest window is fifteen working days; after it passes, the citation and penalty stand as proposed.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 659(a), p. 12
notes.evidence: the citation and the assessment, as proposed, shall be deemed a final order of the Commission and not subject to review by any court or agency
uses: Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission

notes.front: An employer knows its crew works unprotected on a 30-foot open edge, where a fall would probably kill. It has no earlier citations. Which category best fits?
notes.back: C: serious violation.
notes.choices:
A) De minimis violation
B) Other-than-serious violation
C) Serious violation
D) Repeated violation
notes.choicesExplained: A: this bears directly on safety. B: death is a substantial probability. D: there is no history of the same breach.
notes.explanation: The substantial probability of death or serious physical harm, known to the employer, is the test for serious.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 666(k), p. 16
notes.evidence: if there is a substantial probability that death or serious physical harm could result from a condition which exists

notes.front: A breach found on inspection has no direct or immediate relationship to safety or health. What does the Area Director issue?
notes.back: D: a notice of de minimis violations.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, and the case is closed without record
B) A willful citation
C) An imminent danger order
D) A notice of de minimis violations
notes.choicesExplained: B needs a willful breach. C needs a danger of death or serious harm. A: Part 1903 requires a citation or a notice.
notes.explanation: Part 1903 offers either a citation or this notice after the Area Director reviews the inspection report.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.14(a), p. 8
notes.evidence: he shall issue to the employer either a citation or a notice of de minimis violations which have no direct or immediate relationship to safety or health

notes.front: A CSHO finds an excavation about to collapse on workers. Waiting for citations and contests would take weeks. What route does the Act provide?
notes.back: D: the Secretary petitions a district court to restrain the danger.
notes.choices:
A) Wait for the 15-working-day contest period
B) Issue a de minimis notice
C) Refer the case to the state
D) The Secretary petitions a district court to restrain the danger
notes.choicesExplained: A: the danger would outlast the procedure. B: de minimis breaches have no direct relationship to safety. C: the Act gives district courts this power on the Secretary’s petition.
notes.explanation: The court’s order can require steps to remove the danger and bar people from the location.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 662(a), p. 15
notes.evidence: The United States district courts shall have jurisdiction, upon petition of the Secretary, to restrain any conditions or practices in any place of employment

notes.front: A state wants to run its own construction safety programme with standards weaker than the federal ones. Can its plan be approved?
notes.back: B: no, its standards must be at least as effective as the federal ones.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, states have full discretion
B) No, its standards must be at least as effective as the federal ones
C) Yes, if the governor certifies it
D) No, states may never enforce safety standards
notes.choicesExplained: A and C ignore the Act’s test. D is wrong: the Act invites states to submit plans.
notes.explanation: The plan must also include a right of entry at least as effective as the federal one and a ban on advance notice.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 667(c)(2), p. 17
notes.evidence: at least as effective in providing safe and healthful employment and places of employment as the standards promulgated under section 655 of this title

notes.front: How do the civil penalties for a willful violation and a repeated violation differ?
notes.back: Both share the same maximum ($165,514 after 15 January 2025), but only a willful violation carries a minimum ($11,823).
notes.explanation: Part 1903 lists a floor only for willful violations, mirroring section 17(a) of the Act.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.15(d)(2), p. 10
notes.evidence: The penalty per repeated violation under section 17(a) of the Act, 29 U.S.C. 666(a), shall not exceed $165,514.

notes.front: How does an imminent danger differ from a serious violation?
notes.back: A serious violation is a substantial probability of death or serious harm; imminent danger adds that harm could come immediately, before normal enforcement.
notes.explanation: That timing is why imminent danger is dealt with by a court order rather than only by citation and penalty.
notes.source: 29 U.S.C. Chapter 15 (Occupational Safety and Health Act), 2024 edition, § 662(a), p. 15
notes.evidence: which could reasonably be expected to cause death or serious physical harm immediately or before the imminence of such danger can be eliminated through the enforcement procedures

notes.front: What can an employer contest before the Review Commission that employees cannot?
notes.back: The citation itself and the proposed penalty; employees may contest only the reasonableness of the abatement period.
notes.explanation: Both have 15 working days, but Part 1903 gives each a different subject to contest.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1903 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1903.17(a), p. 11
notes.evidence: notify the Area Director in writing that he intends to contest such citation or proposed penalty before the Review Commission
uses: Occupational Safety and Health Review Commission
